ogDesc: Ten Thailand destinations compared by what they're actually good for, so you can pick the right ones and combine them into one trip.
intro: Thailand has more good answers to "where should I go" than most first-time visitors expect, and that's part of the problem — every list gives a different top five and none of them tell you why. This guide compares ten places people actually choose between, by what each is good at rather than by popularity, then shows how to combine more than one into a single trip.
quickAnswerHtml: For most first trips, Bangkok is the starting point, Chiang Mai covers culture and mountains, and the beach half comes down to coast: Phuket or Koh Samui for the most infrastructure, Krabi or Koh Lanta for cliffs and a slower pace. Match the destination to what you actually want — beach, culture, nightlife or nature — rather than trying to fit all of Thailand into one trip.
quickAnswerH2: Where to go in Thailand, decided in one line

blocks.html: There's no single best place to go in Thailand — the country has beach islands, mountain towns, an old royal capital and one enormous capital city, and they're good at different things. The short version: if you want beaches, treat the Andaman and Gulf coasts separately, since they don't share a dry season. If you want culture, Bangkok and Chiang Mai cover most of it, with Ayutthaya close by for temple ruins. If you want nightlife, Bangkok and Pattaya are the obvious two. Below, each type of trip gets its own section with the destinations that actually fit it, followed by how people combine more than one into a single route.

blocks.text: The 10 places most first-timers choose between

blocks.html: These ten names come up again and again when people plan a Thailand trip, so it helps to see them side by side before picking. This isn't a ranking — it's a reference table. Match the "best for" column to what you actually want, then read the sections below for the reasoning.

blocks.caption: Ten Thailand destinations at a glance

blocks.html: Thailand's beaches split across two coasts that don't share a calendar. The Andaman side (Phuket, Krabi, Koh Lanta) is driest from November to April; the Gulf side (Koh Samui) runs on a slightly different pattern with its own wet spell in November. Phuket has the most flights and the widest spread of resort levels, Krabi and Koh Lanta are built around limestone cliffs rather than resort strips, and Koh Samui sits closer to the smaller Gulf islands if you want to add Koh Phangan or Koh Tao.

blocks.html: For temples, ruins and old-town streets, three places do most of the work. Bangkok has the big-name sites — the Grand Palace, Wat Arun — inside a modern city that keeps running around them. Ayutthaya is the old royal capital itself, a short trip from Bangkok, with brick temple ruins you can walk or cycle between. Chiang Mai's old town is smaller and calmer, with dozens of temples inside a square of moat and wall.

blocks.html: Bangkok has the widest range — rooftop bars, live music, night markets that run late — and it doesn't really have an off night. Pattaya is smaller and more concentrated around Walking Street, and it's close enough to Bangkok to visit without a flight. Phuket's nightlife centers on Patong, closer to beach-resort than city.

blocks.html: Chiang Mai and the north have the mountains — cooler air, national parks, waterfalls within a day trip of the city. Pai takes that further into a small valley town with less traffic and more rice fields. Krabi's version of nature is coastal instead: limestone karst, mangroves and island national parks rather than mountains.

blocks.html: Hua Hin is the easiest family base — a long calm beach, an easy drive from Bangkok, and enough resorts built with kids in mind that you're not the exception there. Pattaya covers similar ground with more theme-park-style attractions nearby. Phuket and Bangkok both work too, they just come with more moving parts to manage.

blocks.html: Pai and Chiang Mai keep day-to-day costs low without feeling like you're cutting corners — guesthouses, cafés and street food are all cheap next to the coast. Ayutthaya works well as a low-cost day trip rather than a multi-night stay. Bangkok can be done cheaply too, it just takes more deliberate choices than the north does by default.

blocks.html: This one's short: Chiang Mai has the longest track record as a base for remote work — reliable internet, coworking spaces, and enough long-term visitors that monthly apartment rentals are a normal thing to ask for, not an unusual one. Pai is the smaller, slower alternative, if you want fewer distractions and don't mind a two-to-three-hour drive back to a bigger city when you need one. There isn't a dedicated guide for this yet — for now, the city pages below are the best starting point.

blocks.title: Pick destinations that are already close together
blocks.html: Places near each other are easier to combine without adding a flight. Krabi and Koh Lanta share a province, so you can go by road instead of booking another leg. Pattaya and Bangkok are just a few hours apart by car too. Not every combination needs a domestic flight to work.

blocks.title: Once you've picked, plan the rest
blocks.text: Choosing where to go is the first decision, not the last one. These cover what comes next:

items.label: First time in Thailand
items.note: How many days, when to go, what to book first

faq.q: What's the best first stop when you land in Thailand?
faq.a: Almost everyone starts in Bangkok, since most international flights land there and it works as a hub for domestic flights to everywhere else. Spend 2-3 days there before moving on rather than skipping straight through.

faq.q: Phuket or Koh Samui — which beach island should I pick?
faq.a: Phuket has more flight options, a larger old town, and a wider spread of resort levels. Koh Samui sits closer to Koh Phangan and Koh Tao if you want to add a smaller island, and its main beaches are calmer strips rather than Phuket's mix of bays. Neither is objectively better — it comes down to whether you want more infrastructure (Phuket) or easier onward island-hopping (Samui).

faq.q: Can I do both the mountains and the beach in one trip?
faq.a: Yes, it's the most common route — Bangkok, then Chiang Mai for the north, then one island for the coast. Two short domestic flights connect them. A 10-day trip covers all three at a reasonable pace; with 7 days, pick the city plus one other region rather than trying to fit all three in.

faq.q: Is Krabi or Koh Lanta better for a quieter trip?
faq.a: Koh Lanta is the quieter of the two, since it's an island within Krabi province rather than the province's mainland tourist center. Krabi town and Ao Nang have more restaurants, tour operators and transport links; Koh Lanta trades some of that convenience for calmer beaches and fewer people. Both see some businesses close during the May-October wet season.

faq.q: Where should I go if I only have a long weekend?
faq.a: Pick one destination close to your entry point rather than trying to travel far. From Bangkok, Ayutthaya or Hua Hin both work as short trips without a domestic flight. Pattaya is another close option if nightlife or a beach day is the priority.
